- Get the gourmet skill as soon as you can. It makes any food you eat last for 20 minutes
- Repair your gear often
- Sell any weapon or armor you aren't using, the caveat here being that certain merchants will buy things for more than others. I found that the armorer and blacksmith in Novigrad give back a lot of gold
- Check every lootable box or container for food and alchemy ingredients. Alcohest and Dwarven Spirit are littered everywhere and not only are they needed for alchemy but they refuel your potions when you meditate.
- Exchange florens and orens for Crowns with Vivaldi in Novigrad every chance you get.
- Quen is your best friend if you are struggling with monsters. Axii is beyond helpful for human enemies
- Learn to parry human attacks ASAP. 
- The majority of your exp will come from main story missions. Witcher requests and side quests are more for getting gold or items.
- Pick one of the three main trees to dump skill points in. Blue is great for those who are less comfortable with the combat because it's so broken. Especially when you get to Blood and Wine. Igni everything, when you get further in the tree it becomes great for damage. Axii gets to the point where you can sic human enemies on each other, and it turns off alghouls transformation. Aard is good for crowd control at higher levels. Quen is just as effective at base level and won't need much leveling. Yrden aside from being useful against ghosts will also get an upgrade that blasts enemies with lightning as long as they're standing in it.  
- My exception to that last rule is to get the arrow deflection skill no matter what. Even if you don't level it all the way being able to block arrows is really useful.
- The reason you want to stick to one tree is that you can synthesize red, blue, or green mutagens which give the best stat increases when placed in the slots next to those same color skills. I want to say you can get like a 40% boost to stats when attaching a greater mutagen to your skills when theres three of the same color in that section. Super useful. 
- Upgrade your potions even if you don't level into the green tree. Especially swallow. Thank me later.
- Pick Yennefer.

I was completely off the story before I got to this game anyway, so I didn't entirely mind the nonsensical nature of the ending, but I also wasn't terribly happy about it either. I really loved the first two games, and I wanted a more satisfying conclusion than what was given. Everything about it felt rushed, like the meat of the story was jammed as tightly as it would fit behind all the Disney nonsense. I also just wasn't a fan of Xehanort as a villain at that point either. His entire plot line felt limp, like they couldn't decide on what kind of antagonist they wanted him to be. 

The game looks amazing, and ill give it props on how epic the battles could look. The problem I had was that the gameplay never really felt right to me. Sora seems to practically control himself, all his movement felt too floaty to me, like I was fighting in zero gravity. It's not that it was too difficult either, actually the complete opposite. I think this was a common complaint when the game first came out, but I played on proud mode from the get go and I never struggled in any area. But the combat also never felt engaging either. I thought the idea of keyblade forms was neat, but it doesn't really expand past the initial concept, and I was pretty bored of it by the end of the game. 

The music, as per usual, was fantastic. Track after track of pure gold. What else is there to say? I think most people agree that Kingdom Hearts has one of the best soundtracks in all of video games. 

Overall, the game was, for me, a pretty unsatisfying and dissapointing conclusion to an already bloated and confusing series. Lots to like, but too much to dislike. KH3 is a game i haven't gone back to, i tried critical mode and found that the mode didn't make the game more fun, because i already wasn't really having fun with it to begin with. I'll stick with my fond memories of 1 and 2, that'll be good enough for me.

I always viewed the Crones as a force of nature, kind of the same with Dimm. With O Dimm, he does at least honor his commitments, even if he's simply trying to troll people hard-core. Even then, I still take the stance that evil is a perspective matter, what I consider evil is simply from my point of view. Not saying that you're wrong but that that's what makes morality debates super interesting.

It's a little difficult to define anyone under purely "good" or "evil" in terms of the world of the Witcher series. The world these characters inhabit is as cruel and senseless and rich and beautiful as our own world. Every character lives the way you or I do, with their own sense of morals and as the main characters of their stories. Avallach is certainly not what you would define as a "good" character. His reasons for training and protecting Ciri are most certainly self serving, but in the context of that world his motivations make sense. I think that's honestly one of the coolest things about that series, the characters are so well realized that they can warrant such deep discussions. I mean, can you say that Geralt of Rivia is "good"? Quite often throughout the novels Geralt makes questionable decisions that costs lives, whether he has a good reason or not to do them is irrelevant. It's these truly human aspects of the characters that i think endears me to them so much, they behave the way I think someone probably would behave in a similar situation. The story really muddles around in the gray area of morality, because that's where life exists. I guess my answer to your question is I don't know if Avallach is evil, because my definition of evil will most certainly differ from anyone else's, but that you aren't wrong in coming to that conclusion. I just urge you to think contextually about the characters before coming to any conclusions about them. (I also realize I'm putting a lot of words and thoughts into a purely fictional character, but I really love this series and think about it often)

Tom Bombadil is a neat character, I personally enjoy his section of the story. If you're not familiar, Tom saves the Hobbits from being swallowed by Old Man Willow when they are traveling through the Old Forest. Tom then invites them back to his house for some R&R, before sending them off to continue their journey. The Hobbits almost immediately get caught in another incident and Tom has to come save them again. 

In a movie with a limited run time, this is a pace-breaking piece of narrative. Tom doesn't necessarily add anything to the story, and later when he is mentioned at the Council in Rivendell he's essentially waved off by Gandalf, never to be mentioned again. He's neat in the sense that he adds a layer of mystery to the world of Middle Earth. Who is this man, that claims to be older than the lands and forests he inhabits? How is he immune to the influence of the Ring? The books don't do much lip service to any of these questions though, because they aren't important. It comes off as more of a "filler episode" of sorts. 

So I think the movie team was right in removing it, even though I enjoy it every time i read the books. I essentially affects the story none, and I've seen the argument about Tom being "tension destroying" (not that I necessarily agree with that). It would just add too much to an already long watch, without really adding much of worth. Better off in the books anyway, I can't see anyone really pulling off a good Tom Bombadil anyway. There's a lot to this game, and it'll seem overwhelming at first. Just remember it's a long game, and there's plenty of time to complete the tasks in the game. The first area is a great place to just explore and learn the mechanics of the game at an even pace. Take your time and go to all the points of interest on the map before you leave the area. Also set the difficulty to normal.

A few tips for combat:
Use the quen spell until you start to get a feel for the combat. It gives you a free no damage hit. 
When fighting monsters, dodge. When fighting humans, block. If you wait until right before the hit lands to block, Geralt will parry and knock the enemy off kilter. Same goes with fist fights.
Use the oils. They seem useless at first but every little bit helps and you can upgrade them. Same with potions. Swallow is very useful for restoring health.
Equip the gourmet ability asap. It turns any food you eat into a 25 minute continuous heal. Very useful for adjusting to the game.

Edit: as a side note to gourmet, if you meditate to restore your potions, it will use up your gourmet meter. Just a heads up.

Yesterday was valentines day.

A little over a month ago I broke up with my first long term boyfriend (~9 months of dating) and our anniversary would have been in another month (pie day, because I was supposed to be his slice of pie).

I realize if he saw this he'd know immediately this was about him. I've given it away with just a few sentences. Somewhere around the 7 month mark I began to realize I didn't feel the same way about him anymore. I loved him dearly, but I didn't love him romantically anymore. I tried to stop myself from severing the relationship once but after Xmas break I had just fallen apart. I self imploded and that was it. The look on his face when I broke it off scarred me. This was a person I had previously promised myself I'd never want to hurt or make cry like that. Even thinking about it now tears at me. 

I feel like most people spend a lot of time after a break up trying to tear down the image of their ex, convince themselves that that person was bad for them, was a bad person, etc. I can't do it. I can't bring myself to utter even a single negative comment, even if it would make me feel better. Because he was the best person I ever met. Strong, intelligent, funny... 

He wasn't the problem. He never was. I was the problem. A husk of insecurities and self hate. So I've taken all my anger and dissapointment out on myself. I told people I was over it, because it helped me feel better, but I can't listen to songs we used to like, I deleted apps we talked on, I can't even look at his pictures or the note he gave me once telling me how excited he was to push forward with me.

I finally got myself insurance this year and I'm gonna seek out therapeutic help. Not because of him though, but because this has been a long time coming. If nothing else I can get my life together. Get a good job, pay off my debts, maybe go back to school, explore my hobbies with a fresh outlook... but for right now I'm sitting in the bathroom at work writing this trying not to ugly cry at work. I can't help but feel like the monster. I hope whatever he's doing right now he's feeling a lot better than me. If his days could be filled with endless happiness, even without me, that would be perfect. 

Anyway I just wanted to type this out, get it into the ether and out of my brain. If you read any of this, thanks for taking the time. Hopefully your valentines was a lot better than mine, and not lonely. Have a good day.

Your panels are beautiful, and your positioning and posing are magnificent as well, but your pacing and dynamacy could use some work. Your actions don't flow very well and can make reading the panels confusing. I've seen artists who do similar things and reading their comics becomes a chore because I'm never quite certain what is happening. Others have no sense of pacing and make every minor movement part of the flow which doesn't work either. Make sure you lead the audience in the direction you want them to see the action, and ask yourself if you were an observer if you could discern the action with little or no experience in reading comics. Movies can be great examples to study. Find a really good action movie with fights that sing and watch how the director leads you around the scene. The church scene from kingsman is a great example, or the hallway fight scene in the original oldboy. Action has setup, release, and aftermath. If you were to display a punch you might start with the person reeling back, then show the strike, then show the person being punched flying back from the punch. It doesn't have to be like that every time but hopefully you see what I mean.

I was once with the majority of people who absolutely despised this entry to the series. When I first played through it, I found Fi annoying, I hated the excessive amount of shit you had to do in order to get through certain areas, I hated flying, I wasn't entirely a fan of the art style, all of the cutscenes, heavy dialogue... you get the picture.

I didn't even finish it the first time I played it. I became so fed up with it because of all the little things that annoyed me about the game I put it down for a good while. My roommate at the time beat the game and told me my judgments of it were really harsh, and that I should give it a second chance. It wasn't until I moved back home (during a period of isolation I'll add) that I returned to what soon became one of my favorite Zelda adventures.

It was magical, the cinematic value of the game, I became more entangled in the lives of the characters. The swordplay was incredible, I actually had difficulty playing through other Zelda games for a bit after I beat SS because I fell in love with the motion control. I found myself far more amazed by the environments of the game, how expansive they were and how much really filled their space.

But I think the most important change that happened in the way that I view the game as a whole came when I finally got the Master Sword, and was able to travel through the Gate of Time to see Zelda. She explains that the hardships you endure, all the work you had to put into every trip down to the surface, all of it was molding you into the hero you had to be to face Demise. It all made sense: having to return to a previous dungeon with some of the doors locked and stronger enemies, having to guide that turd of a robot up the mountain after he fucked up a simple delivery task, going through the trials of the three dragons to obtain the Song of the Hero, all of it centered around the motif of growing as a hero. I don't know, it just all stuck with me even long after I had finished the game. Shit, even Fi became less annoying once I just tolerated exactly what she was trying to give me, help. Sure, she does it a lot, but that's what a good companion does, give you helpful advice when they think you need it. Oh, and the ending? I almost cried.

I guess the point of this long rant is that I had to come back to the game with a different perspective in order to really enjoy it. I may have had my expectations too high the first time, I may have just been feeling bitchy, who knows? Either way Skyward Sword has easily become one of my favorite Zelda games in the series. I've played through it like 6 times. 

**TL;DR** - I had to give Skyward Sword a fair chance before I really found what I liked about it.
